pharm: Topical antibacterial, antifungal and antiprotozoal agent
quick: Topical: apply to affected skin 2-4 times daily
Use only if clearly needed; avoid extensive use
Neurologic/visual symptoms with extensive use; thyroid function tests
summary: Quiniodochlor (clioquinol; iodochlorhydroxyquin) is a halogenated 8-hydroxyquinoline with topical antibacterial, antifungal and antiprotozoal activity, used for superficial skin infections, athlete's foot, tinea and inflammatory dermatoses, often combined with a corticosteroid. The oral form is NOT FDA-approved - it was restricted/withdrawn for internal use because of SMON (subacute myelo-optic neuropathy), a severe neurotoxic syndrome of peripheral neuropathy and optic atrophy reported especially in Japan. It stains skin, hair and fabric yellow, can interfere with thyroid function tests, and must be kept away from the eyes. Only topical use persists in some markets.
indications: Topical treatment of superficial fungal and bacterial skin infections (athlete's foot/tinea pedis, ringworm)
Inflammatory skin disorders (eczema/dermatitis), frequently in combination with a corticosteroid
Historical (obsolete) oral use for intestinal amebiasis and nonspecific diarrhea

dosage.d: Apply 3% cream or ointment to the affected area 2-4 times daily
dosage.n: Often combined with hydrocortisone or other corticosteroid

dosage.d: Historically ~250 mg three times daily (no longer used)
dosage.n: Oral use withdrawn due to SMON / neurotoxicity

admin: For external (topical) use only - apply a thin layer to affected, intact skin
Do not apply to large surface areas or broken/eroded skin (increases absorption)
Note: stains skin, hair and clothing/fabric yellow
moa: Quiniodochlor is a metal-ion chelator/ionophore that chelates trace metals (iron, copper, zinc) required by microorganisms, exerting antibacterial, antifungal and antiprotozoal activity. As an 8-hydroxyquinoline it also interferes with microbial enzymes involved in DNA replication.

absolute: Oral/systemic use (contraindicated owing to neurotoxicity / SMON)
relative: Application to large or broken/eroded skin areas

preg: Use only if clearly needed and avoid extensive topical application. Systemic use is not recommended given iodine absorption and neurotoxicity concerns.
lact: Use with caution during breastfeeding and avoid extensive topical use.
renal: Use with caution where systemic absorption could occur (e.g., extensive or broken skin).
hepatic: Use with caution or avoid in hepatic disease/impairment.

moderate: Thyroid function tests - its iodine content elevates protein-bound iodine and can alter results, appearing within a week of application to extensive or eroded skin and persisting with prolonged use
minor: Ferric chloride-based urine tests (e.g., for phenylketonuria) may be affected
interactions.diagnostics: Elevates protein-bound iodine and the free thyroxine index; may affect certain colorimetric urine tests.

common: Local skin irritation, itching or rash
Yellow staining of skin, hair and clothing/fabric
serious: SMON (subacute myelo-optic neuropathy) with systemic/oral use - ascending sensory-motor peripheral neuropathy with optic neuritis/atrophy and visual loss
Thyroid enlargement or dysfunction from iodine load
emergency: Acute neurotoxicity with visual loss or paralysis (systemic exposure)

monitoring: With prolonged or extensive topical use, watch for neurologic or visual symptoms (numbness, tingling, weakness, visual change)
Be aware of altered thyroid function tests (protein-bound iodine) during prolonged use
Discontinue if neuropathy or visual changes occur
counsel: For external use only and keep away from the eyes
It stains skin, hair and clothing yellow
Do not apply to large or broken areas of skin
Report any numbness, tingling, weakness or change in vision
Tell your clinician it can affect thyroid blood tests
pk: Local antimicrobial action at the application site
Topical absorption generally low through intact skin
Store at room temperature, protected from light
pearls: Oral form NOT FDA-approved - FDA restricted internal use; oral use withdrawn worldwide after SMON (~10,000 cases, mostly Japan, 1955-1970)
Stains skin, hair and fabric yellow and can interfere with thyroid function tests (protein-bound iodine)
Topical use only in current practice; avoid large/broken skin areas to limit absorption
missed: For topical use, apply when remembered and resume the regular schedule; do not double up.
overdose: There is no specific antidote. Management is symptomatic and supportive. Systemic toxicity is dominated by neurotoxicity (SMON-type) - discontinue the drug and provide supportive care.
